questions.question: Which modern Git command removes a file from the staging area without deleting your edits?
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged <file>` takes the file out of the staging area while leaving your edits in your working directory intact.

questions.question: Which command discards all unstaged edits in `app.js` and reverts it to the last commit?
questions.explanation: `git restore <file>` overwrites the working copy with the version from the last commit or staging area.

questions.question: Which command allows you to change the message of your most recent commit?
questions.explanation: `git commit --amend` lets you combine staged changes or update the commit message of the most recent commit.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?

options.A: `git reset` works only on GitHub, while `git revert` works only locally
options.B: `git reset` rewrites history by moving the branch pointer back, while `git revert` creates a new commit that inverts past changes
options.C: `git revert` deletes files, while `git reset` renames them

questions.explanation: `git revert` is non-destructive because it adds a new commit undoing previous changes, making it safe for shared branches.

questions.question: Why is `git reset --hard` considered dangerous?

options.B: It permanently deletes all uncommitted changes and overwrites your working directory
options.C: It locks the repository on GitHub

questions.explanation: `--hard` forces Git to match the target commit exactly, destroying uncommitted edits in both the working directory and staging area.

questions.question: If you have already pushed commits to a shared team repository on GitHub, how should you undo a bad commit?
questions.explanation: Always use `git revert` on public branches so teammates don't experience broken history or divergent branch conflicts.

questions.question: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1` do?

options.A: Deletes the last commit and all its changes forever
options.B: Undoes the last commit but keeps all changes staged ready to commit again
options.C: Reverts all changes to the original clone state

questions.explanation: `--soft` moves HEAD back by one commit while leaving all changes staged in the index.

questions.question: What does `HEAD~1` mean in Git syntax?

options.A: The first commit ever made in the repo
options.B: One commit before the current HEAD commit (the parent commit)

questions.explanation: The tilde `~` operator navigates ancestry: `HEAD~1` is the immediate parent commit, `HEAD~2` is two commits back.

questions.question: What happens if you run `git restore .` in your project folder?

options.A: All unstaged changes in tracked files across the current folder are discarded
options.D: All files are staged for commit

questions.explanation: `git restore .` discards unstaged modifications in tracked files, reverting them to their last committed state.

questions.question: What command removes untracked files that are cluttering your directory?
questions.explanation: `git clean -f` forces the deletion of untracked files in the working directory (use with caution!).
